strengths: Addresses three well-motivated issues in RL-based alpha mining (reward sparsity, sequential structural representation, mode collapse/diversity) with a coherent combined solution: an RGCN encoder over AST representations plus a GFlowNet generator with a multi-component reward (IC, structure-aware alignment, novelty) and entropy regularization.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across three markets (CS1300, CS1500, S&P500) against seven baselines spanning traditional ML, GP, RL-based, and generative approaches, with both correlation-based and portfolio-based metrics.
Detailed ablation study (Table 2) that incrementally adds each proposed component (ES, GNN, SA, NOV, ENT) and shows monotonic-ish improvement, helping to isolate contributions.

Sensitivity analysis over reward-weighting hyperparameters and pool size/training steps, showing smooth behavior and comparison of GFlowNet vs. PPO training dynamics (faster, lower-variance convergence).

Includes a theoretical appendix formalizing why reducing pairwise alpha correlation reduces OLS estimator variance and improves conditioning, providing some formal grounding for the diversity motivation.
Reasonably thorough appendices with metric definitions, hyperparameters, operator/feature tables, baseline descriptions, and pseudocode, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Despite diversity/novelty being a central motivating claim, the paper never reports a direct, quantitative diversity metric for the generated alpha pool (e.g., average pairwise correlation, redundancy statistics before vs. after combination); the novelty reward is only validated indirectly through downstream IC/portfolio metrics.

No indication of statistical significance or variance across multiple random seeds/runs; all reported numbers appear to be single-run point estimates, which is concerning given known instability of RL/GFlowNet training and financial backtests.

The theoretical result in Appendix E (Proposition E.1) is essentially a standard OLS/ridge variance-under-collinearity derivation and does not provide novel insight specific to the proposed GFlowNet method; it reads as generic textbook material used to motivate diversity rather than a genuine technical contribution.

The S&P500 evaluation window ends in 2020 due to stated data limitations, which is dated for a paper likely submitted in 2025/2026 and weakens the practical relevance of the US-market results; also, US and China test windows are non-overlapping and inconsistent in length, complicating cross-market comparison.

Absolute IC values (~0.05-0.09) are modest and typical of many published alpha-mining baselines; the paper does not discuss transaction costs, turnover, or capacity/liquidity constraints, which are critical for assessing real-world tradability of the reported high Sharpe ratios (e.g., SR up to 6.32 on S&P500 seems unusually high and warrants scrutiny/discussion).

Several recently cited LLM-based alpha-mining approaches (Chain-of-Alpha, AlphaAgent, etc.) are discussed in related work but excluded from the empirical baseline comparison, leaving open how AlphaSAGE compares to this contemporary and increasingly relevant class of methods.

The combination stage simply reuses an existing method (AlphaForge) rather than being a novel contribution, so the core technical novelty is confined to the encoder and GFlowNet reward design; the incremental nature of this contribution should be weighed against the complexity of the overall pipeline.

Limited discussion of computational cost/scalability of the RGCN+GFlowNet training relative to baselines (e.g., wall-clock time, number of trajectories needed), which matters for practical adoption in quantitative research pipelines.

strengths: Clear identification of three concrete limitations of prior RL-based alpha mining (reward sparsity, sequential/structure-blind representations, mode collapse from single-objective RL) and a framework (AlphaSAGE) that maps directly onto each: RGCN over ASTs for structure, GFlowNets for diversity-seeking generation, and a dense multi-component reward.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: four markets/universes (CSI300, CSI500, CSI1000, S&P500), seven diverse baselines spanning traditional ML, GA, RL, GAN-based, and LLM-based alpha mining methods, plus both correlation-based and portfolio-based metrics.

Thorough ablation and sensitivity analysis (component ablation table, reward-weight sensitivity, MaxLen, encoder depth, hidden dimension, reward-schedule shape, encoder architecture comparison RGCN vs. Transformer, and a 2x2 RL/GFlowNet x structure-aware disentanglement study) that isolates the contribution of each design choice.

Additional robustness checks that are often missing in similar papers: multi-seed variance analysis, runtime/scalability comparison, and learning-dynamics comparison against PPO showing faster/more stable convergence.

A supporting theoretical appendix (Proposition F.1 and Corollary F.2) formalizing why lower cross-alpha correlation reduces estimator variance and improves conditioning, giving some principled backing to the diversity motivation.

Reasonably transparent reporting, including an appendix section (E.8) that candidly discusses cases where cumulative-return curves are less dominant despite superior IC-based metrics, rather than hiding mixed results.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a recombination of existing components (RGCN, GFlowNets with trajectory balance, KNN-based structure-behavior alignment reward) applied to a specific application domain; the methodological novelty relative to prior GFlowNet/GNN literature is incremental rather than fundamental.

The claim in Section 3.4 that the three reward components are automatically 'compatible' and do not compete is asserted rather than empirically or theoretically demonstrated; in practice IC-maximization and novelty/diversity objectives can trade off, and this tension is not rigorously analyzed beyond the sensitivity plots.

Some result tables show AlphaSAGE not uniformly best on every sub-metric (e.g., CSI1000 RIC where AlphaQCM appears competitive/better), yet the narrative frames the method as ranking first across the board; a more nuanced discussion of where and why it doesn't win would strengthen credibility.

The appendix rationalization of weaker cumulative-return performance on CSI1500 and S&P500 (attributing it to regime shifts and IC not perfectly mapping to path-dependent P&L) reads as a post-hoc explanation for underperformance rather than a pre-registered analysis, which weakens the strength of the central claim that structure/diversity-aware mining reliably improves realized portfolio outcomes.

The U.S. market backtest data ends in 2020/2021 (explicitly noted as a data-source limitation), which is a fairly stale window for a paper published in 2025/2026 and limits confidence that findings hold in more recent, higher-rate, higher-volatility regimes.

Several relevant recent baselines mentioned in the related-work/reference list (e.g., QuantFactor REINFORCE, Chain-of-Alpha, trajectory-level reward shaping methods) are not included as empirical baselines, leaving open whether AlphaSAGE's gains hold against the most recent competitors.

The theoretical appendix (Proposition F.1) is a fairly standard linear-algebra result about OLS variance under correlated regressors; while it nicely motivates diversity, it is not a novel technical contribution and its connection to the actual GFlowNet-driven diversity mechanism used in the method is only qualitative.

Reproducibility relies on a code repository link that is not shown to be populated/verifiable in the reviewed manuscript, and several implementation details (e.g., exact novelty-reward pool update dynamics, threshold for pool inclusion) are described only briefly in the pseudocode.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: it clearly diagnoses three interlocking problems in RL-based alpha mining (reward sparsity, sequential/flat representation of expressions, and mode collapse toward a single high-reward alpha) and proposes matching solutions (dense multi-faceted reward, RGCN-on-AST encoder, GFlowNet sampler).

Experimental coverage is broad: four market universes (CSI300/500/1000, S&P500), correlation and portfolio-level metrics, comparisons against 7-8 recent and relevant baselines (including 2025 methods such as AlphaForge, AlphaQCM, AlphaAgent).

Extensive ablations and sensitivity studies (component ablation in Table 2, reward-weight sensitivity in Fig. 4, MaxLen/encoder-depth/hidden-dim sweeps in Appendix E.2, reward-schedule sensitivity, encoder-architecture comparison RGCN vs Transformer, RL-vs-GFlowNet disentanglement in Table 10) go well beyond what many papers in this area report, and support the claim that gains are not attributable to a single component or a lucky hyperparameter choice.
Robustness checks such as multi-seed evaluation (Table 12) and runtime/scalability comparison (Table 11) add credibility to the empirical claims.

The appendix provides a clear textbook-style derivation connecting alpha diversity/decorrelation to estimator variance reduction, which nicely motivates why explicit novelty rewards are useful for portfolio construction (even if the underlying result is classical).
weaknesses: Novelty is largely a combination of existing components (RGCN encoders, GFlowNets, multi-term reward shaping) applied to the alpha-mining domain rather than a fundamentally new modeling or algorithmic idea; the theoretical contribution in Appendix F is a standard multicollinearity/OLS-variance result that, while well presented, is not new and mainly justifies an already well-known heuristic (diversify weakly-correlated signals).

The backtesting protocol differs across markets in ways that are not well justified (top-20% long-only for CSI300/500/1000 vs. top/bottom-10% long-short for S&P500), which complicates fair comparison and raises the possibility that protocol choices were tuned to favor the proposed method on each dataset.

The narrative sometimes overstates what the figures show: e.g., in Fig. 6 (S&P500) AlphaForge visibly leads AlphaSAGE for most of 2018-2020 and only converges/exceeds near the very end, yet the text describes AlphaSAGE as tracking 'near the top' and 'recovering faster' throughout; similarly Fig. 5 curves are closely overlapping despite claims of a 'clear lead.' Appendix E.8 offers a post-hoc regime-shift narrative to explain why cumulative-return curves don't match the (very large) tabulated IC/portfolio gains, which feels like rationalization rather than rigorous analysis.

The claim that the three reward components (R_IC, R_SA, R_NOV) are 'compatible' and do not conflict is asserted by construction/sign argument but never empirically verified (e.g., no reported correlation or gradient-conflict analysis between the terms during training).

US market backtest data stops at end of 2020 due to data-source limitations, meaning the method's performance on more recent, more volatile regimes (2021-2024) is untested for the U.S., limiting the generality of the S&P500 results relative to the CSI300/500/1000 results (which extend to 2024).

The framework has many interacting hyperparameters (λ_max, η_max, β entropy coefficient, SA/NOV weights, MaxLen, pool capacity, encoder depth, hidden dim, schedule shape), and although sensitivity plots suggest broad plateaus on CSI300, all such tuning/validation is shown only on this single market, leaving open whether the 'low tuning burden' claim generalizes.
There is no analysis of transaction costs, turnover, or capacity constraints, which are central practical concerns for a paper positioned as being useful for constructing tradable alpha portfolios.

It is unclear whether baseline methods (especially very recent ones like AlphaForge, AlphaQCM, AlphaAgent) were tuned with comparable care/effort as the proposed method beyond using their default settings, which raises reproducibility and fairness concerns given the uniformly large margins by which AlphaSAGE outperforms essentially every baseline on every metric across all four markets.

strengths: The paper tackles three well-motivated and concrete limitations of existing RL-based alpha mining (reward sparsity, sequential/structure-agnostic encoding, mode collapse to a single alpha) and proposes coherent, targeted solutions: an RGCN encoder over ASTs, a GFlowNet generator for diverse sampling, and a dense multi-faceted reward (IC + structure-aware + novelty).

Extensive empirical evaluation across four markets (CSI300/500/1000 and S&P500) and against a wide range of strong, recent baselines (traditional ML, GP, AlphaGen, AlphaQCM, AlphaForge, AlphaAgent), with consistent first-rank results on correlation and portfolio metrics.

Thorough ablation and sensitivity analysis: component-wise ablation (ES/GNN/SA/NOV/ENT), reward-weight sensitivity, encoder depth/hidden-dim sensitivity, MaxLen sensitivity, encoder architecture comparison (RGCN vs Transformer), RL-vs-GFlowNet disentanglement, multi-seed stability, and runtime/scalability comparisons — this is unusually comprehensive for the venue and substantially strengthens the empirical claims.

A supporting theoretical appendix formally connects alpha diversity to estimator variance/conditioning in the downstream linear combiner, providing some principled justification for the diversity-seeking design (though the result itself is largely a standard multicollinearity argument).

Clear qualitative discussion of subperiod performance under regime shifts, which honestly acknowledges cases where cumulative-return curves are less dominant despite strong IC-based metrics, improving transparency of the evaluation.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily a combination of existing components (RGCN, GFlowNet with trajectory balance, KNN-based novelty/structure rewards) applied to alpha mining; the individual techniques are well established, so the contribution is more integrative/engineering than conceptually new.

The theoretical appendix (Proposition F.1) largely restates standard OLS multicollinearity/variance-inflation results rather than deriving a genuinely new theoretical insight specific to the proposed method; its connection to the actual reward design (RSA, RNOV) is only loosely argued informally in the main text ("Compatibility of reward components") rather than formally justified.

No statistical significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals or hypothesis tests) is reported for the main Table 1 results across all four markets; multi-seed variance is only reported for CSI300 in the appendix, leaving robustness on CSI500/CSI1000/S&P500 less well supported.

Backtesting protocol details (e.g., transaction costs, slippage, turnover) are not discussed, which is important given the reliance on AR/Sharpe/MDD for claims of practical portfolio superiority; absence of cost modeling could materially affect the reported advantage.

Overlap/redundancy between the structure-aware reward (behavioral alignment via embedding neighbors) and the novelty reward (correlation with pool members) is not analyzed — both rely on similarity in overlapping spaces, and the paper does not clarify how much unique signal each contributes beyond the ablation table.

The US market data is capped at 2020, limiting relevance to more recent regimes, and the paper's own regime-shift discussion suggests IC-based objectives may not reliably translate to cumulative portfolio outperformance in shorter, stressed windows, somewhat softening the practical claims.
Code repository link is left blank in the abstract, and while this may be an anonymization artifact, it limits ability to verify reproducibility during review.
